screens.title: Control Flow: Conditional Statements
screens.narratorSegment: In programming, decision points are what make software behave differently for different situations. In this lesson you will learn the primary Java constructs for branching: the if family, nested checks, the switch statement with its break and fall-through rules, and the ternary operator for concise decisions. You'll see why we choose one construct over another, how fall-through can cause subtle bugs, and when a compact ternary helps readability. We'll practice with concrete code: a grade ladder, a leap year checker that combines multiple logical tests, and a simple menu implemented with switch. Along the way you'll learn a few common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting curly braces, misusing string equality, and omitting break statements. By the end you will be able to read conditions, predict which branch runs, and write clear, testable branching logic. Think of this chapter as giving your program the ability to answer questions at runtime — and you'll leave knowing how to ask those questions precisely and safely.

screens.title: What is control flow?
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow is the rulebook a program follows as it runs: by default statements are executed sequentially, but conditional statements provide decision points that change that order. In Java the simplest such decision is an if test: a boolean expression is evaluated and the associated block executes only when the expression is true. This matters because real programs must respond to different inputs, states, or errors; without conditionals your code would always do the same thing. A concrete example: checking a temperature value and printing a message only when it exceeds a threshold. A common misconception is thinking conditionals are only for branching big algorithms; in reality they appear everywhere — input validation, feature toggles, error handling, and UI state. Another pitfall is assuming evaluation order inside complex expressions; Java evaluates boolean expressions left to right for the operators you use, but mixing side effects into tests makes code harder to reason about. Key takeaway: control flow lets your program ask questions at runtime, and designing those questions clearly makes behavior predictable and testable. What is control flow? means control flow determines which statements run next; conditionals introduce branching based on boolean tests.. In practical terms, how conditional statements change execution order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is control flow?
Control Flow: the program's decision points
Sequential execution vs conditional branching.
Key Takeaway
Branching makes programs dynamic; structure conditions so their truth is easy to test.
Definition
Control flow is the order in which individual statements or instructions execute. Conditionals change that order by choosing which block runs based on a boolean expression.
Concrete example
int temperature = 25;
if (temperature > 20) {
  System.out.println("It's a warm day!");
}
Common misconception
Don't assume conditionals are only for big decisions. Small checks prevent errors and control state transitions throughout an application.
Where it matters
  • Validating inputs before processing them.
  • Routing logic in command-line menus or UI choices.
  • Feature toggles and configuration-driven behavior.
Key Takeaway

Design your tests and order checks so each branch is obvious and easy to test. Avoid side effects inside complex boolean expressions.

screens.title: The if statement
screens.narratorSegment: The if statement is the basic building block for branching. It evaluates a boolean expression and executes the following block only when that expression is true. This allows you to guard actions, validate values, and short-circuit work that would be unnecessary or invalid. A key style recommendation is to always use curly braces even for single statements to avoid accidental mis-scoping when you add lines later. For example, checking a temperature and printing a message demonstrates the simple case. You should also be careful about what you put inside the condition: avoid side effects like modifying variables in the test, because it makes behavior harder to predict and test. A concrete practice is to assign any intermediate boolean expression to a well-named boolean variable and then use that variable in the if test for clarity. Common errors include forgetting braces and mismatching relational operators. As a final thought, write unit tests for both true and false paths so you can confirm both behaviors — that habit prevents many subtle bugs. The if statement means use if to run code only when a boolean condition is true; prefer braces and clear boolean names for readability.. In practical terms, execute code only when a boolean condition is true. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › The if statement
Code Walkthrough
int temperature = 25;
if (temperature > 20) {
  System.out.println("It's a warm day!");
}

// Good practice: name boolean for clarity
boolean isWarm = (temperature > 20);
if (isWarm) {
  System.out.println("Wear light clothes.");
}
Always prefer braces and consider intermediate variables for complex tests. This aids readability and testing.
Explainer points
  • If evaluates a boolean expression; true executes its block.
  • Use braces to avoid errors when adding lines later.
  • Avoid side effects inside the condition for predictability.
Common Mistake
Omitting braces causes only the first line to be conditional, often producing logic bugs when more lines are added.
Key Takeaway

If statements are explicit guards. Keep conditions simple and test both true and false paths.

screens.title: If-Else and Else-If Ladder
screens.narratorSegment: When you need an alternative when a condition is false, use else. For multiple mutually exclusive outcomes, chain else if checks as an else-if ladder. The ladder evaluates each condition in order and executes the block of the first condition that is true, skipping the rest. A practical example is mapping numeric grades to letter grades: check for A, then B, then C, and default to F. Order matters: place the most specific or highest-priority tests first to avoid incorrect matches. A common misconception is thinking else-if evaluates in parallel; it does not — it stops at the first true test. For maintainable code, keep each condition simple and prefer range checks that are clear to read. Also add a final else to handle unexpected values if appropriate. Always test boundary values such as exact cutoffs (70, 80, 90) to ensure the code prints the expected grade. This pattern gives predictable, prioritized selection among several possibilities. If-Else and Else-If Ladder means use if–else if–else to evaluate conditions in order and run the first matching branch; ordering and tests must be deliberate.. In practical terms, choosing one path among many sequential checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › If-Else Ladder
Grade Example
int grade = 85;
if (grade >= 90) {
  System.out.println("Grade: A");
} else if (grade >= 80) {
  System.out.println("Grade: B");
} else if (grade >= 70) {
  System.out.println("Grade: C");
} else {
  System.out.println("Grade: F");
}
Because grade is 85, the grade >= 80 branch triggers and the rest are skipped. Test edge cutoffs carefully.
Steps to design a ladder
  1. List outcomes and their priority.
  2. Order tests from highest priority to lowest.
  3. Use an else for unexpected values when appropriate.
Misconception
Else-if chains are not parallel checks. The first true condition stops further evaluation.
Key Takeaway

Use ordered checks for mutually exclusive choices. Keep boundaries explicit and test cutoffs.

screens.title: Nested if statements and logical operators
screens.narratorSegment: Nested if statements let you express conditions that depend on previous checks. For example, you might first check whether a user has a license, and inside that block check the user's age before allowing them to drive. While nesting is powerful, too much nesting makes code hard to read and maintain. Often you can replace nested checks by combining conditions with logical operators: use && for 'and' and || for 'or'. For instance, a rule that requires both license and minimum age can be written as a single if with &&, which flattens structure and often improves clarity. A common mistake is creating deeply nested branches that duplicate logic; instead extract boolean helper variables or methods with descriptive names. Another pitfall is incorrect grouping: use parentheses to make precedence explicit when mixing && and ||. Always write tests that cover every branch, including the inner branches in nested structures. The learner takeaway is to prefer clear, shallow structures and explicit boolean names when possible. Nested if statements and logical operators means use nesting when logically necessary; prefer combined conditions or helper variables to reduce depth and improve clarity.. In practical terms, compose multi-layered conditions and combine tests with && and ||. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Nested if & Logical Operators
Nested Example
boolean hasLicense = true;
int age = 18;
if (hasLicense) {
  if (age >= 18) {
    System.out.println("You are eligible to drive.");
  } else {
    System.out.println("You have a license, but are too young to drive alone.");
  }
} else {
  System.out.println("You need a license to drive.");
}
Combined with &&
if (hasLicense && age >= 18) {
  System.out.println("You are eligible to drive.");
} else if (hasLicense) {
  System.out.println("You have a license, but are too young to drive alone.");
} else {
  System.out.println("You need a license to drive.");
}
Combining conditions flattens structure and often makes tests easier to read. Use parentheses to clarify complex precedence.
Common Mistake
Deep nesting duplicates logic and increases cognitive load. Extract helper functions when logic repeats.
Key Takeaway

Prefer clear boolean names and shallow condition structures; combine conditions when it improves readability and testing.

screens.title: Switch statement and case labels
screens.narratorSegment: The switch statement evaluates a single expression and jumps to the matching case label, making it a tidy alternative to long if-else-if ladders when you compare one variable against many discrete values. Java switch supports int, byte, short, char, String, and enum. Each case labels a block of code; when matched, execution continues until a break is found or the switch ends. That fall-through behavior can be useful intentionally but is a frequent source of bugs when a break is omitted by accident. Always include a default case to handle unexpected values, which makes your code more defensive. A standard menu example prints a message for each numeric choice and uses break to stop further execution. Choose switch when you compare the same variable to many constants, but prefer if-else for range checks like grade thresholds. When migrating code, switch can improve readability for clear, discrete options and makes adding new choices straightforward. Switch statement and case labels means use switch for discrete-choice selection; remember break prevents fall-through and default handles unexpected values.. In practical terms, select among many discrete values cleanly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Switch usage
keyIdea.text: Use switch for discrete-choice selection; remember break prevents fall-through and default handles unexpected values.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Switch & Case
Menu Example
int dayOfWeek = 3; // 1=Monday, 2=Tuesday, etc.
switch (dayOfWeek) {
  case 1:
    System.out.println("Monday");
    break;
  case 2:
    System.out.println("Tuesday");
    break;
  case 3:
    System.out.println("Wednesday");
    break;
  default:
    System.out.println("Weekend");
    break;
}
Use switch for many fixed alternatives; prefer if for ranges. Include default to handle unexpected values.
When to use switch
  • Multiple discrete constant comparisons on the same expression.
  • Cleaner than long if-else chains for many options.
  • Not suited for range checks.
Pro Tip
Group related cases intentionally when you want the same behavior for multiple values, but add comments if fall-through is intentional.
Key Takeaway

Switch improves readability for discrete choices. Always include default and use break to control flow intentionally.

screens.title: Break and fall-through: a common pitfall
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent beginner mistake in switch statements is forgetting the break keyword. Without break, execution falls through to subsequent cases until a break or the end of the switch is reached. This can produce surprising output. Consider a switch on a character command: if case for 'S' prints Start but omits break, execution continues into the 'P' case and prints Pause as well. Sometimes fall-through is intentional, for example to group multiple labels to execute the same code, but it must be explicit and documented with comments. To find issues, test each case value and also test values near the intended ones. When debugging, run the program with instrumented prints to see which cases execute. Fixing missing break statements is usually the correct remediation unless you intentionally want shared behavior. Finally, remember that break only exits the switch; it does not exit enclosing loops unless you use labeled breaks. Write unit tests that assert exactly the expected outputs for each case to catch fall-through bugs early. Break and fall-through: a common pitfall means omitting break causes fall-through: subsequent case blocks execute until a break or switch end, often producing bugs.. In practical terms, how an omitted break can execute unexpected cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fall-through
keyIdea.text: Omitting break causes fall-through: subsequent case blocks execute until a break or switch end, often producing bugs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Break and Fall-through
Assessment Example (no break)
char command = 'S';
switch (command) {
  case 'S':
    System.out.println("Start");
  case 'P':
    System.out.println("Pause");
    break;
  case 'R':
    System.out.println("Resume");
    break;
  default:
    System.out.println("Unknown Command");
    break;
}
When command is 'S', this prints Start then Pause because the break after Pause stops further fall-through. The missing break after Start caused the additional print.
Debug checklist
  • Test each case value separately.
  • Check for missing break when an extra case executes.
  • Document intentional fall-through with a comment.
Common Mistake
Accidental fall-through prints unintended outputs. Always review new cases for break placement.
Key Takeaway

Use break to control switch flow. If you intentionally fall through, add a clear comment so readers know it was deliberate.

screens.title: Ternary operator
screens.narratorSegment: The ternary operator offers a compact way to express a simple if-else assignment in one line. Its syntax is condition? expressionIfTrue : expressionIfFalse. Use it for short decisions that are easy to read at a glance, like assigning a pass/fail label based on a score. For example, assigning a result to a string in one line makes code shorter, but be careful: nested ternaries quickly become unreadable. If the conditional logic has more than two outcomes or includes side effects, prefer a normal if-else block for clarity. Another common source of confusion is using ternary expressions for statements that have side effects like printing; ternary is best for expressions that produce a value. When in doubt, favor readability. A practical style is to use the ternary for very simple assignments and add a short comment when it improves comprehension. Always run tests for both branches to ensure the resulting value is correct. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Ternary Operator
Compact assignment example
int studentScore = 55;
String result = (studentScore >= 60) ? "Pass" : "Fail";
System.out.println("Student result: " + result);
This single line replaces a simple if-else assignment. Avoid ternary for complex logic or side effects.
Guidelines
  • Use for single-value assignments only.
  • Prefer if-else when logic has multiple statements or branches.
  • Avoid nested ternaries; prefer named methods instead.
Key Takeaway

Ternary is a readability tool for short expressions. Use it sparingly and test both outcomes.

screens.title: Leap Year Checker & Menu System
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through two small programs that combine the chapter's ideas. First, the Leap Year Checker: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 400, or if it is divisible by 4 but not by 100. That translates into a single if using logical operators: (year % 400 == 0) || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100!= 0). Test with 2000, 1900, and 2024 to cover the edge cases. Second, the Menu System uses switch to select among actions. You should print a welcome and the available choices, then switch on the chosen number. Include cases for 1, 2, 3 and a default accepting any other input. Remember break after each case to prevent fall-through. A useful habit is to run the menu with invalid inputs to ensure default is executed. These exercises teach combining operators, ordering checks, and defensively handling unexpected values. After coding, refactor if you find duplicated logic and add unit tests for boundary and unexpected inputs to catch regressions. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Hands-on Activity
LeapYearChecker (template)
public class LeapYearChecker {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int year = 2024; // Test with 1900, 2000, 2024

    // A year is leap if divisible by 400
    // OR divisible by 4 AND not divisible by 100
    if ((year % 400 == 0) || (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0)) {
      System.out.println(year + " is a leap year.");
    } else {
      System.out.println(year + " is NOT a leap year.");
    }
  }
}
Test edge cases: 2000 should be leap, 1900 not leap, 2024 leap.
MenuSystem (template)
public class MenuSystem {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int choice = 2; // Test with 1, 2, 3, 99

    System.out.println("Welcome to the Game!");
    System.out.println("1. New Game");
    System.out.println("2. Load Game");
    System.out.println("3. Options");
    System.out.println("Please enter your choice: " + choice);

    switch (choice) {
      case 1:
        System.out.println("Starting a new game...");
        break;
      case 2:
        System.out.println("Loading saved game...");
        break;
      case 3:
        System.out.println("Displaying options...");
        break;
      default:
        System.out.println("Invalid choice. Please select 1, 2, or 3.");
        break;
    }
  }
}
Run with different choices to confirm correct behavior and that default handles unexpected values.
Key Takeaway

These two small programs force you to combine boolean logic, order conditions, and use switch and break correctly. Run tests for all interesting values to catch edge cases early.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: We can summarize this chapter into a few compact ideas. First, control flow is how code chooses what to run; conditionals make programs responsive. Second, the if family — if, else, else if — evaluates boolean expressions in order and runs the first matching block. Third, nested ifs express layered decisions, but prefer combined conditions or helper booleans to reduce depth. Fourth, switch is ideal for many discrete options; always include break to avoid unwanted fall-through and provide a default as a safety net. Fifth, the ternary operator writes short conditional assignments compactly but should not replace readable if-else blocks in complex cases. Finally, testing edge cases and using clear naming are your best defenses against common bugs. Holding these concepts together will let you design branching logic that is predictable, testable, and maintainable.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Before you move on, keep three compact reminders in mind. First, always use braces for if and else blocks to avoid accidental scoping mistakes. Second, when using switch, include break unless you intentionally want fall-through, and always provide a default branch. Third, favor readability: use the ternary for short value assignments only, and refactor nested ifs into combined conditions or helper methods when it clarifies intent. These habits reduce common errors and make your conditional logic easier to test and maintain. As you practice the two hands-on exercises, watch for edge cases and write small tests for each branch. That discipline will pay off quickly when your programs handle real input robustly. Always use braces

fullNarratorScript:
In programming, decision points are what make software behave differently for different situations. In this lesson you will learn the primary Java constructs for branching: the if family, nested checks, the switch statement with its break and fall-through rules, and the ternary operator for concise decisions. You'll see why we choose one construct over another, how fall-through can cause subtle bugs, and when a compact ternary helps readability. We'll practice with concrete code: a grade ladder, a leap year checker that combines multiple logical tests, and a simple menu implemented with switch. Along the way you'll learn a few common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting curly braces, misusing string equality, and omitting break statements. By the end you will be able to read conditions, predict which branch runs, and write clear, testable branching logic. Think of this chapter as giving your program the ability to answer questions at runtime — and you'll leave knowing how to ask those questions precisely and safely.

By the end of this chapter you will: implement if, else, and else if statements to create branching logic, and understand when to use each form. You'll practice nested if statements so you can express multi-layered business rules, and learn how to combine conditions with logical operators to keep logic clear. You will apply the switch statement for efficient selection between many discrete values, and learn to use break and default correctly to prevent common bugs like fall-through. Finally, you'll use the ternary operator to write compact conditional assignments for simple cases, without sacrificing readability. Each objective pairs a coding example and a short practice task so you can prove competency. For example, you will implement a leap year checker that requires combined conditions, and a simple menu implemented with switch where you must place break statements correctly. These skills matter because conditional logic appears in every program: input validation, routing, configuration choices, and business rules. Mastering them reduces bugs and makes code easier to test and maintain.

This second objectives screen lists concrete practice tasks you will do and why each matters. First, implement the leap year checker using combined conditions; this teaches how to translate a textual rule into logical operators and order checks to avoid mistakes. Second, build the menu system with switch; practice placing break statements and a default branch so the program handles unexpected input gracefully. Third, refactor a nested if scenario into combined conditions with logical operators to improve readability and reduce nesting. Fourth, replace a simple if-else assignment with the ternary operator and discuss when this makes code clearer or less clear. These tasks are chosen because writing, running, and testing each small program gives immediate feedback about your understanding. You will test edge cases such as years divisible by 100 but not 400, invalid menu options, and overlapping conditions. Completing these tasks confirms you can not only read conditional logic but also design and test it reliably.

Control flow is the rulebook a program follows as it runs: by default statements are executed sequentially, but conditional statements provide decision points that change that order. In Java the simplest such decision is an if test: a boolean expression is evaluated and the associated block executes only when the expression is true. This matters because real programs must respond to different inputs, states, or errors; without conditionals your code would always do the same thing. A concrete example: checking a temperature value and printing a message only when it exceeds a threshold. A common misconception is thinking conditionals are only for branching big algorithms; in reality they appear everywhere — input validation, feature toggles, error handling, and UI state. Another pitfall is assuming evaluation order inside complex expressions; Java evaluates boolean expressions left to right for the operators you use, but mixing side effects into tests makes code harder to reason about. Key takeaway: control flow lets your program ask questions at runtime, and designing those questions clearly makes behavior predictable and testable. In practical terms, how conditional statements change execution order. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The if statement is the basic building block for branching. It evaluates a boolean expression and executes the following block only when that expression is true. This allows you to guard actions, validate values, and short-circuit work that would be unnecessary or invalid. A key style recommendation is to always use curly braces even for single statements to avoid accidental mis-scoping when you add lines later. For example, checking a temperature and printing a message demonstrates the simple case. You should also be careful about what you put inside the condition: avoid side effects like modifying variables in the test, because it makes behavior harder to predict and test. A concrete practice is to assign any intermediate boolean expression to a well-named boolean variable and then use that variable in the if test for clarity. Common errors include forgetting braces and mismatching relational operators. As a final thought, write unit tests for both true and false paths so you can confirm both behaviors — that habit prevents many subtle bugs. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. When you need an alternative when a condition is false, use else. For multiple mutually exclusive outcomes, chain else if checks as an else-if ladder. The ladder evaluates each condition in order and executes the block of the first condition that is true, skipping the rest. A practical example is mapping numeric grades to letter grades: check for A, then B, then C, and default to F. Order matters: place the most specific or highest-priority tests first to avoid incorrect matches. A common misconception is thinking else-if evaluates in parallel; it does not — it stops at the first true test. For maintainable code, keep each condition simple and prefer range checks that are clear to read. Also add a final else to handle unexpected values if appropriate. Always test boundary values such as exact cutoffs (70, 80, 90) to ensure the code prints the expected grade. This pattern gives predictable, prioritized selection among several possibilities. Nested if statements let you express conditions that depend on previous checks. For example, you might first check whether a user has a license, and inside that block check the user's age before allowing them to drive. While nesting is powerful, too much nesting makes code hard to read and maintain. Often you can replace nested checks by combining conditions with logical operators: use && for 'and' and || for 'or'. For instance, a rule that requires both license and minimum age can be written as a single if with &&, which flattens structure and often improves clarity. A common mistake is creating deeply nested branches that duplicate logic; instead extract boolean helper variables or methods with descriptive names. Another pitfall is incorrect grouping: use parentheses to make precedence explicit when mixing && and ||. Always write tests that cover every branch, including the inner branches in nested structures. The learner takeaway is to prefer clear, shallow structures and explicit boolean names when possible. The switch statement evaluates a single expression and jumps to the matching case label, making it a tidy alternative to long if-else-if ladders when you compare one variable against many discrete values. Java switch supports int, byte, short, char, String, and enum. Each case labels a block of code; when matched, execution continues until a break is found or the switch ends. That fall-through behavior can be useful intentionally but is a frequent source of bugs when a break is omitted by accident. Always include a default case to handle unexpected values, which makes your code more defensive. A standard menu example prints a message for each numeric choice and uses break to stop further execution. A frequent beginner mistake in switch statements is forgetting the break keyword. Without break, execution falls through to subsequent cases until a break or the end of the switch is reached. This can produce surprising output. Consider a switch on a character command: if case for 'S' prints Start but omits break, execution continues into the 'P' case and prints Pause as well. Sometimes fall-through is intentional, for example to group multiple labels to execute the same code, but it must be explicit and documented with comments. To find issues, test each case value and also test values near the intended ones. When debugging, run the program with instrumented prints to see which cases execute. Fixing missing break statements is usually the correct remediation unless you intentionally want shared behavior. Finally, remember that break only exits the switch; it does not exit enclosing loops unless you use labeled breaks.
